claim: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are responsible for persistent renewal of blood and immune cells throughout a lifetime.
source: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are responsible for persistent renewal of blood and immune cells throughout a lifetime.
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational studies (Spangrude et al., 1988; Baum et al., 1992; Seita and Weissman, 2010) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: HSCs have the ability to self-renew and differentiate into effector cells in response to physiological demands such as infection or bleeding.
source: They have the ability to not only self-renew, but also differentiate into effector cells in response to physiological demands such as infection or bleeding (Figure 1A; Spangrude et al., 1988; Baum et al., 1992; Seita and Weissman, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and reference to Figure 1A showing the hematopoietic hierarchy.

claim: HSC clones sustaining several driver mutations inhibit differentiation, drive proliferation, block programmed cell death and phagocytosis, and outcompete normal HSCs.
source: HSC clones sustaining several driver mutations inhibit differentiation, drive proliferation, block programmed cell death and phagocytosis, and outcompete normal HSCs (Tomasetti et al., 2017; Jan et al., 2012; Miyamoto et al., 2000; Jamieson et al., 2004; Rossi et al., 2008; Pang et al., 2013; Busque et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on HSC mutations and their effects.

claim: The initiating driver mutations in HSCs can lead to clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), which predisposes individuals to blood diseases and atherosclerosis.
source: The initiating driver mutations in HSCs on their own can lead to clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), which predisposes an individual to these blood diseases, as well as atherosclerosis, and affects a significant percentage of aging populations (Jaiswal et al., 2017; Jaiswal et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on CHIP and its clinical implications.

claim: mRNA abundance and protein abundance are not always well correlated.
source: Furthermore, it has been well documented that mRNA abundance and protein abundance are not always well correlated (Gygi et al., 1999; Koussounadis et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies documenting the discordance between mRNA and protein levels.

claim: mRNA translation studies in HSCs suggest multiple modes in the regulation of protein abundance.
source: mRNA translation studies in HSCs suggest multiple modes in the regulation of protein abundance, and therefore mRNA levels of genes of interest may be insufficient for determining protein levels in HSCs (Buszczak et al., 2014; Signer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on mRNA translation in HSCs.

claim: HSCs have increased sensitivity to protein misfolding and a restricted capacity for proteasomal turnover.
source: Signer and co-workers have also recently reported increased sensitivity to protein misfolding and a restricted capacity for proteasomal turnover in the HSC compartment (Hidalgo San Jose et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study by Signer and colleagues.

claim: A total of 7917 genes encoding proteins were detected across all cell types analyzed.
source: Across all cell types we detected a total of 7917 genes encoding proteins expressed and detectable in HSCs and their progenitors (Supplementary file 1, Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data presented in the supplementary tables.

claim: The adult HSC compartment had the least protein diversity, with 4030 proteins detected.
source: The adult HSC compartment had the least protein diversity, with 4030 proteins detected (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1C and the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: There is a general trend of increased protein diversity during the differentiation process, with MPPs and OPPs expressing larger numbers of distinct proteins compared to HSCs.
source: We observed a general trend in increased protein diversity during the differentiation process, with MPPs and OPPs expressing larger numbers of distinct proteins compared to HSCs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1C comparing protein numbers across cell types.

claim: The increased protein diversity during differentiation differs from transcriptomic reports where HSCs present increased mRNA diversity compared to their progeny.
source: This result differs from transcriptomic reports where HSCs present increased mRNA diversity in the stem cell compartment compared to their progeny (Ramos et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim compares the current proteomic findings to previously published transcriptomic data.

claim: Principal component 1 isolates HSCs from all other cell types in PCA analysis.
source: Excitingly, each component played a distinct role in separating cell types from one another: component 1 isolates HSCs from all other cell types, whereas component 2 separates stem and multipotent progenitors from the more-committed oligopotent progenitor compartment (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Supplementary file 1, Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 1D and supplementary figures.

claim: Principal component 2 separates stem and multipotent progenitors from the more-committed oligopotent progenitor compartment.
source: Excitingly, each component played a distinct role in separating cell types from one another: component 1 isolates HSCs from all other cell types, whereas component 2 separates stem and multipotent progenitors from the more-committed oligopotent progenitor compartment (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Supplementary file 1, Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 1D and supplementary figures.

claim: cKit was detected across all cell types with levels high in HSCs, MPPs and lower in CLPs and GMPs.
source: As expected, cKit was detected across all cell types with levels high in HSCs, MPPs and lower in CLPs and GMPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data and is consistent with known expression patterns.

claim: CD150/Slamf1 abundance was exclusive to HSC and MPPa compartments.
source: CD150/Slamf1 abundance was exclusive to HSC and MPPa compartments, an attestation to the purity of these sorted samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in the supplementary figure and validates sample purity.

claim: Ly6d, a marker of early B-cell progenitors, was uniquely detected in the CLP compartment.
source: Ly6d, a marker of early B-cell progenitors, was uniquely detected in the CLP compartment (Figure 1F; Ghaedi et al., 2016; Inlay et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data in Figure 1F and citations to studies identifying Ly6d as a B-cell progenitor marker.

claim: Ki67 was lowly detected in the HSC compartment with a steady increase in abundance in the MPP compartment and highest in the OPPs.
source: The cell-cycle associated protein Ki67 was lowly detected in the HSC compartment with a steady increase in abundance in the MPP compartment and highest in the OPPs (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Flt3 was exclusively detected in MPPc and CLP.
source: We exclusively detected Flt3 in MPPc and CLP, CD16/32 in GMP and (very lowly) CMP, and IL7Ra in CLP (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: CD16/32 was detected in GMP and very lowly in CMP.
source: We exclusively detected Flt3 in MPPc and CLP, CD16/32 in GMP and (very lowly) CMP, and IL7Ra in CLP (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: IL7Ra was detected in CLP.
source: We exclusively detected Flt3 in MPPc and CLP, CD16/32 in GMP and (very lowly) CMP, and IL7Ra in CLP (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Sca1 was not detected in any of the datasets.
source: Similar to previous studies by Trumpp and co-workers, we were not able to detect Sca1 in any of our datasets (Cabezas-Wallscheid et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Proteins associated with cell cycle and DNA damage repair were significantly less abundant in HSCs compared to progenitor cells.
source: Proteins associated with cell cycle and DNA damage repair were significantly less abundant in HSCs compared to progenitor cells, and both processes have been shown to be dramatically reduced in the HSC compartment (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 6; Nijnik et al., 2007; Pietras et al., 2011; Rossi et al., 2007a; Rossi et al., 2007b).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in the figures and citations to studies on HSC cell cycle and DNA repair.

claim: Approximately 80–90% of HSCs are quiescent.
source: Given that approximately 80–90% of HSCs are quiescent, we anticipated lower levels of DNA repair-associated response in our dataset (Rossi et al., 2007b; Sudo et al., 2000; Tesio et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on HSC quiescence.

claim: The double-strand DNA repair protein Rad51 is not detected in HSC proteomics data but is detected in all other cell types.
source: For example, the double-strand DNA repair protein Rad51 is not detected in our HSC proteomics data but is detected in all other cell types. (Supplementary file 1, Tables 1 and 2; Beerman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data in the supplementary tables and a citation to a study on DNA repair in HSCs.

claim: Esam levels were very high in HSCs and MPPas with decreased abundance in MPPbs and no detection for the remaining cell types.
source: In our dataset, Esam levels were very high in HSCs and MPPas with decreased abundance in MPPbs and no detection for the remaining cell types (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Esam expression pattern detected by mass spectrometry was recapitulated in flow cytometry analysis.
source: This result was recapitulated in flow cytometry analysis of Esam levels, further supporting the quality of the proteomics dataset. (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the validation experiment shown in Figure 2A and supplementary figure.

claim: Average Pfkl levels were decreased in the HSC compartment compared to MPPa and MPPb.
source: We also validated differential abundance of the regulatory glycolytic enzyme phosphofructokinase (Pfkl) by fluorescence microscopy (Figure 2B and C). Average Pfkl levels were decreased in the HSC compartment compared to MPPa and MPPb.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Dnmt3a was not detected in any HSC replicates but was well detected in MPP and OPP populations.
source: We noted that DNA-methyl transferase 3a (Dnmt3a) was not detected in any of our HSC replicates but was well detected in MPP and OPP populations (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 1, Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2D and supplementary tables.

claim: Freshly-sorted HSCs were both Ki67 negative and Dnmt3a negative compared to LSK cells that were positive for both proteins.
source: This finding was further validated by microscopy where freshly-sorted HSCs or a mixed population of stem and progenitor cells (LSK: Lin-, Sca1+, cKit+) were stained with anti-Ki67 and anti-Dnmt3a. HSCs were both Ki67 negative and Dnmt3a negative compared to LSK cells that were positive for both proteins (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mutations in Dnmt3a expression are among the most common mutations found in hematologic malignancies and pre-AML mutations in HSCs.
source: Mutations in Dnmt3a expression have been implicated as disease-initiating mutations in hematologic malignancies and are among the most common mutations found in disease pathologies, including pre-AML mutations in HSCs (Corces-Zimmerman et al., 2014; Jan et al., 2012; Ley et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2015) and in CHIP (Jaiswal et al., 2017; Jaiswal et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on Dnmt3a mutations in blood diseases.

claim: Self-renewal is perpetual in the absence of Dnmt3a and expression is required for differentiation.
source: Self-renewal is perpetual in the absence of Dnmt3a and expression is required for differentiation (Challen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on Dnmt3a function in HSCs.

claim: In the absence of Dnmt3a, genes promoting self-renewal are not repressed, preventing differentiation.
source: DNA methylome analysis has shown that in the absence of Dnmt3a, genes promoting self-renewal are not repressed, therefore preventing differentiation (Challen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on Dnmt3a and DNA methylation in HSCs.

claim: Cultured HSCs have increased levels of Ki67 and Dnmt3a compared to freshly-sorted HSCs.
source: To this end, HSCs were sorted and cultured under media conditions promoting cell cycle (Wilkinson et al., 2019). Fluorescence microscopy revealed that cultured HSCs have increased levels of Ki67 and Dnmt3a (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2E comparing fresh and cultured HSCs.

claim: Dnmt3a protein is not present in G0 quiescent HSCs but is accumulated as HSCs enter cell cycle.
source: Our findings support a scenario where Dnmt3a protein is not present in G0 quiescent HSCs but is accumulated as HSCs enter cell cycle in order to silence stem-associated genes and enable HSC differentiation into multipotent or oligopotent cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing Dnmt3a absence in quiescent HSCs and presence in cycling HSCs.

claim: Non-cycling HSCs likely do not synthesize Dnmt3a rather than synthesize the protein only to rapidly degrade it.
source: Given the sensitivity of HSCs to perturbations in protein synthesis and turnover, we further hypothesize that non-cycling HSCs likely do not synthesize Dnmt3a rather than synthesize the protein only to rapidly degrade it (Hidalgo San Jose et al., 2020; Signer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from the data and citations to studies on HSC protein synthesis.

claim: Igf1r is not detected in young adult HSC mass spectrometry data but is detectable in the MPPs.
source: Insulin-like growth factor one receptor (Igf1r) has been shown to be undetectable by single-cell staining in the HSC compartment compared to MPPs (Venkatraman et al., 2013). Similarly, Igf1r is not detected in our young adult HSC mass spectrometry data but is detectable in the MPPs (Supplementary file 1, Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data and comparison to a previous study.

claim: CD81 was not detected in young adult bone marrow-resident HSCs but was found in all other cell types analyzed.
source: Lin, Goodell and co-workers have shown that the proliferation-associated protein CD81 is found on HSCs that have moved into cycle (Lin et al., 2011). In our studies, CD81 was not detected in young adult bone marrow-resident HSCs, which appear to have a more quiescent signature, but was found in all other cell types analyzed (Supplementary file 1, Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data and comparison to a previous study on CD81 in HSCs.

claim: Over 40% of proteins (3130 proteins in total) were detected across all cell types.
source: Over 40% of proteins were detected across all cell types, 3130 proteins in total (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: 619 proteins were absent in the HSC compartment but were found in all other cell types.
source: For example, 619 proteins were absent in the HSC compartment but were found in all other cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data analysis.

claim: 340 proteins were exclusively found in the GMP compartment.
source: In investigating uniquely-expressed proteins, particularly the 340 proteins exclusively found in the GMP compartment, we identified GMP-specific proteins including CCAAT-enhancer-binding protein ε (Cebpe), Adhesion G Protein-Coupled Receptor G3 (Adgrg3) and Membrane-spanning 4-domains, subfamily A, member 3 (Ms4a3), all of which have previously been reported to be associated with macrophage and granulocyte-specific lineage commitment (Supplementary file 1, Tables 1-3; Goardon et al., 2011; Hsiao et al., 2018; Ishibashi et al., 2018; Nakajima et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data and citations to studies on GMP-specific proteins.

claim: Igf2bp2 was detected as a uniquely-expressed protein in the HSC compartment.
source: In the HSC compartment, Igf2bp2 was detected as a uniquely-expressed protein, as has previously been identified as differentially expressed by HSCs compared to MPP1s (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3; Cabezas-Wallscheid et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in the supplementary figures and comparison to a previous study.

claim: Across both datasets (current study and Cabezas-Wallscheid et al.), a total of 6466 proteins were detected in HSCs and/or MPPas/MPP1s, with 70.43% overlap.
source: Across both datasets, a total of 6466 proteins were detected in HSCs and/or MPPas/MPP1s, with 70.43% overlap (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of the current mass spectrometry data to a previous study.

claim: Of the 49 differentially abundant proteins identified by Cabezas-Wallscheid et al. that were also detected in the current datasets, 37 were consistently differentially abundant across both experimental methods.
source: Of the 49 differentially abundant proteins identified by Cabezas-Wallscheid et. al. that were also detected in our datasets, 37 were consistently differentially abundant across both experimental methods (at least 2-fold more frequently detected in HSC or early progenitor in our data, or denoted as differentially expressed per Cabezas-Wallscheid et. al.).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of the current mass spectrometry data to a previous study.

claim: 5434 proteins were detected in old mouse HSCs, a 35% increase in protein diversity compared to young adult mouse HSCs.
source: Data analysis revealed detection of 5434 proteins in old mouse HSCs, a 35% increase in protein diversity compared to young adult mouse HSCs, with comparable protein numbers detected across the young and old adult MPP compartments (Figure 3A, and Supplementary file 1, Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3A comparing young and old HSCs.

claim: Old mouse HSCs lose the distinctness of young adult mouse HSCs along principal component 1.
source: PCA analysis demonstrated the high similarity between young and old adult mouse HSCs as compared to progenitor cells but also important differences across both component 1, where old mouse HSCs lose the distinctness of young adult mouse HSCs, and component 2, where old mouse HSCs to occupy a unique protein signature in comparison to both young adult stem and progenitor compartments (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1, Table 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 3B comparing young and old HSCs.

claim: Old mouse HSCs occupy a unique protein signature along principal component 2 in comparison to both young adult stem and progenitor compartments.
source: PCA analysis demonstrated the high similarity between young and old adult mouse HSCs as compared to progenitor cells but also important differences across both component 1, where old mouse HSCs lose the distinctness of young adult mouse HSCs, and component 2, where old mouse HSCs to occupy a unique protein signature in comparison to both young adult stem and progenitor compartments (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1, Table 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 3B comparing young and old HSCs.

claim: cKit levels were on average higher in old cells compared to their young adult counterparts.
source: cKit levels were on average higher in the old cells compared to their young adult counterparts, which has also been observed by others (Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1, Tables 1 and 2; Beerman et al., 2010; Mann et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3C and citations to previous studies.

claim: CD150hi HSCs are myeloid biased, and this sub-population increases most-dramatically in old mice.
source: Earlier FACS separation of CD150hi and CD150lo HSCs revealed CD150hi HSCs are myeloid biased, and this sub-population increases most-dramatically in old mice (Beerman et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on CD150 expression in HSCs.

claim: The range of CD150 levels was lowest in young adult mouse HSCs.
source: Our proteomics data revealed similar variations in CD150 levels, with the range lowest in young adult mouse HSCs (Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1, Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ki67 detection was still lower in the old HSC compartment compared to that of young adult and old downstream progenitors, although more frequently detected than the young adult HSC compartment.
source: Additionally, Ki67 detection was still lower in the old HSC compartment compared to that of young adult and old downstream progenitors, although more frequently detected than the young adult HSC compartment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: There was an increase in Ki67 abundance in old MPPbs compared to young adult MPPbs.
source: We also detected an increase in Ki67 abundance in old MPPbs compared to young adult MPPbs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data comparing young and old MPPbs.

claim: von-Willebrand Factor (vWF) is associated with myeloid and platelet biases during hematopoiesis.
source: von-Willebrand Factor (vWF) is associated with myeloid and platelet biases during hematopoiesis, and we also detected increased vWF in old mouse HSCs and MPPas (Figure 3D; Grover et al., 2016; Mann et al., 2018; Pinho et al., 2018; Sanjuan-Pla et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3D and citations to studies on vWF in hematopoiesis.

claim: Increased vWF was detected in old mouse HSCs and MPPas.
source: von-Willebrand Factor (vWF) is associated with myeloid and platelet biases during hematopoiesis, and we also detected increased vWF in old mouse HSCs and MPPas (Figure 3D; Grover et al., 2016; Mann et al., 2018; Pinho et al., 2018; Sanjuan-Pla et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Integrin surface proteins are critical in mediating a pro-inflammatory response that can elicit bias in HSC fate determination.
source: Integrin surface proteins are critical in mediating a pro-inflammatory response that can elicit bias in HSC fate determination, and such proteins are also well documented to increase during aging in addition to inflammatory events (Gekas and Graf, 2013; Haas et al., 2015; Mann et al., 2018; Pang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on integrin proteins in HSCs.

claim: Itga2b (CD41) was detected in old mouse HSCs.
source: We detected Itga2b (CD41) in old mouse HSCs, which has been demonstrated to induce a myeloid bias, but, similar to Mann et. al., we did not see a significant difference between young and old adult (Supplementary file 1, Tables 1 and 2) (Gekas and Graf, 2013; Mann et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data and comparison to a previous study.

claim: Levels of Itgb3 (CD61) increased in the old compartments of HSCs, MPPas and MPPbs.
source: However, levels of the complementary signaling molecule Itgb3 (CD61) increased in the old compartments of HSCs, MPPas and MPPbs, as described previously by Regev, Baltimore and co-workers (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Mann et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in the supplementary figure and citation to a previous study.

claim: Old mouse HSCs had lower levels of abundance of proteins associated with cell cycle and DNA damage repair compared to progenitors.
source: Additionally, we performed gene set enrichment analysis and identified that, like young adult mouse HSCs, old mouse HSCs had lower levels of abundance of proteins associated with cell cycle and DNA damage repair (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Compared to young adult mouse HSCs, cell cycle and DNA damage repair-associated proteins were more enriched in old HSCs.
source: However, compared to young adult mouse HSCs, cell cycle and DNA damage repair-associated proteins were more enriched in the old cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene set enrichment analysis comparing young and old HSCs.

claim: The diversity of mRNAs was similar across cell types despite much lower protein diversity in HSCs.
source: The diversity of mRNAs was similar across cell types despite much lower protein diversity in HSCs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of RNA-seq and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The correlation between protein and mRNA was lowest in the HSC compartment (ρ = 0.300).
source: The correlation was lowest in the HSC compartment (ρ = 0.300), with comparable levels between MPPs (Figure 4B and C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Spearman correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The correlation values between protein and mRNA are similar to what has been previously reported for a mixed population of human HSCs and MPPs.
source: Importantly, these correlation values are similar to what has been previously reported for a mixed population of human HSCs and MPPs (Amon et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to a previous study on human HSCs and MPPs.

claim: Pearson correlation of genes detected as mRNA and protein in all four cell types revealed largest difference in fold changes when comparing HSC to MPP values.
source: Pearson correlation of genes that were detected as mRNA and protein in all four cell types revealed largest difference in fold changes (normalized protein intensity/mRNA TPM) when comparing HSC to MPP values, but less so between MPPs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Pearson correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: mRNA translation is uniquely regulated in the HSC compartment at least in part through a mechanism other than altered gene transcription.
source: These analyses support previous reports by Signer and co-workers that mRNA translation is uniquely regulated in the HSC compartment at least in part through a mechanism other than altered gene transcription (Hidalgo San Jose et al., 2020; Signer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis and citations to previous studies on mRNA translation in HSCs.

claim: Of the proteins that were not detected in HSCs despite the presence of mRNA, a large number of them were unique to HSCs—more so than by random chance compared to MPPs.
source: We observed that of the proteins that were not detected in HSCs despite the presence of mRNA, a large number of them were unique to HSCs—more so than by random chance compared to MPPs (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A and supplementary figure comparing observed to expected values.

claim: The lower diversity of proteins in HSCs is likely attributed to biological, rather than technical, reasons.
source: This suggests that the lower diversity of proteins in HSCs is likely attributed to biological, rather than technical, reasons.
evidence: This is inferred from the statistical analysis showing non-random distribution of undetected proteins in HSCs.

claim: Dnmt3a and Adnp are genes where message and protein abundance are decoupled uniquely in the HSC compartment.
source: This list of genes where message and protein abundance are decoupled uniquely in the HSC compartment include Activity-dependent neuroprotector homeobox (Adnp) and Dnmt3a, among others (Figure 4F, Supplementary file 1, Table 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4F comparing mRNA and protein levels.

claim: mRNA transcripts of Dnmt3a and Adnp were detected in the HSC compartment at comparable levels to that of MPPs, but protein levels were markedly reduced for Adnp and absent for Dnmt3a in HSCs.
source: While mRNA transcripts of Dnmt3a and Adnp were detected in the HSC compartment at comparable levels to that of MPPs, protein levels were markedly reduced for Adnp and absent for Dnmt3a in HSCs (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4F comparing mRNA and protein levels.

claim: The mRNA and protein levels of housekeeping protein Hprt1 were consistent across all cell types.
source: However, the mRNA and protein levels of our housekeeping protein Hprt1 were consistent across all cell types (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4F for Hprt1.

claim: There is a marked decrease in rates of translation in HSCs.
source: Previous literature reports highlight a marked decrease in rates of translation (Jarzebowski et al., 2018; Signer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on translation rates in HSCs.

claim: There is a reduction in abundance of proteins associated with ribosome biogenesis in the HSC compartment.
source: Enrichment analysis of our mass spectrometry data also reveals a reduction in abundance of proteins associated with ribosome biogenesis in the HSC compartment (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Total RNA content in HSCs is approximately 1 pg/cell.
source: Comparable to previous reports, we determined total RNA content in HSCs to be approximately 1 pg/cell and a significant increase in total RNA content in all progenitor populations in comparison after normalization with respect to cell size (Figure 5B, Signer et al., 2014; Jarzebowski et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5B and citations to previous studies.

claim: There is a significant increase in total RNA content in all progenitor populations compared to HSCs after normalization with respect to cell size.
source: Comparable to previous reports, we determined total RNA content in HSCs to be approximately 1 pg/cell and a significant increase in total RNA content in all progenitor populations in comparison after normalization with respect to cell size (Figure 5B, Signer et al., 2014; Jarzebowski et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Lower levels of ribosomal proteins were detected in young adult mouse HSCs by mass spectrometry.
source: By mass spectrometry we detected lower levels of ribosomal proteins in young adult mouse HSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Rates of translation and potentially lower ribosome component abundance are in part responsible for regulating reduced protein abundance in the young adult HSC compartment.
source: Taken together, these data further support a scenario where rates of translation and potentially lower ribosome component abundance are in part responsible for regulating reduced protein abundance in the young adult HSC compartment.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on translation rates, ribosomal protein levels, and total RNA content.

claim: Across the transcriptome of HSCs and MPPs, approximately 86% of genes are potential targets of miRNAs for all cell types.
source: Across the transcriptome of HSCs and MPPs ~ 86% of genes are potential targets of miRNAs for all cell types according to the miRDB database (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis using the miRDB database shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Within the list of genes that are putative targets of miRNA, genes that are uniquely detected at the mRNA level but absent at the protein level are more enriched in the HSC dataset than by random chance (881 in total).
source: Within the list of genes that are putative targets of miRNA, genes that are uniquely detected at the mRNA level but absent at the protein level are more enriched in the HSC dataset than by random chance (881 in total) (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C and supplementary figure.

claim: The mRNA expression values of unique genes in the HSC compartment do not deviate strongly compared to mRNA expression values in MPPs.
source: The mRNA expression values of these unique genes in the HSC compartment do not deviate strongly compared to mRNA expression values in MPPs, and therefore transcriptional regulation cannot sufficiently explain the absence of their low detection by mass spectrometry (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in the supplementary figure comparing mRNA levels.

claim: Within the fourth quartile of miRNAs with the highest overlaps with uniquely undetected HSC proteins, known miRNAs implicated in mouse HSC and early hematopoiesis biology were identified, such as Mir29a, Mir25a, Mir125b and Mir130a.
source: Within the fourth quartile of miRNAs with the highest overlaps, we saw known miRNAs implicated in mouse HSC and early hematopoiesis biology, such as Mir29a, Mir25a, Mir125b and Mir130a (Figure 5D and Supplementary file 1, Table 10; Bissels et al., 2012; Chung et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2010; Guo and Scadden, 2010; Hu et al., 2015; O'Connell et al., 2010; Ooi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5D and citations to studies on these miRNAs in HSCs.

claim: Mir29a has been shown to be highly expressed in HSCs compared to progenitor cells and has been implicated in negatively regulating Dnmt3a levels, promoting self-renewal.
source: Notably, we have previously shown Mir29a to be highly expressed in HSCs compared to progenitor cells, and it has been implicated in negatively regulating Dnmt3a levels, in turn, promoting self-renewal (Han et al., 2010; Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Mir29a function in HSCs.

claim: Deletion of Mir29a has been shown to decrease self-renewal and increase HSC cycling.
source: Deletion of Mir29a has been shown to decrease self-renewal and increase HSC cycling (Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on Mir29a deletion in HSCs.

claim: Mir551 has been shown to be expressed in human HSCs and MPPs and is a negative prognostic indicator in acute myeloid leukemia.
source: We also identified Mir551. While Mir551 expression has not been validated in mouse HSCs, it has been shown to be expressed in human HSCs and MPPs and is a negative prognostic indicator in acute myeloid leukemia (de Leeuw et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on Mir551 in human HSCs and AML.

claim: Of the 881 uniquely undetected young adult HSC proteins that are putative targets of miRNAs, 776 (88%) are detected in old mouse HSCs.
source: Of the 881 uniquely undetected young adult HSC proteins that are putative targets of miRNAs, 776 (88%) are detected in old mouse HSCs, with 105 still undetected (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5E comparing young and old HSC proteomes.

claim: Ribosomal proteins were more readily detected in the old HSC compartment compared to the young adult compartment.
source: Notably, ribosomal proteins were more readily detected in the old HSC compartment compared to the young adult compartment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Young adult mouse HSCs show the lowest enrichment of proteins associated with epigenetic regulation of gene expression and ribosome biogenesis, with levels in old mouse HSCs comparable to those of progenitors.
source: Enrichment analysis of Gene Ontology genesets reveals the lowest enrichment of proteins associated with epigenetic regulation of gene expression and ribosome biogenesis in young adult mouse HSCs, with levels in old mouse HSCs comparable to those of progenitors (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene set enrichment analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The regulatory mechanism of old mouse HSCs for protein abundance is more similar to MPPs, with increased reliance on epigenetic regulation of transcription and perhaps increased translational capacity.
source: This suggests a model in which the regulatory mechanism of old mouse HSCs for protein abundance is more similar to MPPs, with increased reliance on epigenetic regulation of transcription and perhaps increased translational capacity, although this has not yet been well studied.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the enrichment analysis data comparing young and old HSCs.

claim: Young adult mouse HSCs have more open chromatin than progenitor cells.
source: It has been reported that HSCs have more open chromatin than MPPs, suggesting an increased plasticity in gene transcription (Buenrostro et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on chromatin accessibility in HSCs.

claim: mRNA translation is markedly reduced and highly sensitive to perturbations in the HSC compartment.
source: Conversely, mRNA translation is markedly reduced and highly sensitive to perturbations in the HSC compartment, and we now report a lower correlation between mRNA and protein (Signer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study and the current correlation analysis.

claim: Primary regulatory mechanisms of stemness shift downstream of gene transcription towards translation specifically in the young adult HSC compartment.
source: We therefore propose that perhaps primary regulatory mechanisms of stemness shift downstream of gene transcription towards translation specifically in the young adult HSC compartment (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the combined data on chromatin accessibility, translation rates, and mRNA-protein correlation.

claim: In a mixed population of human HSCs and MPPs, the correlation between mRNA and protein for genes critical for stem-cell maintenance was markedly reduced compared to more-committed progenitor populations.
source: These results are further supported by previous studies in a mixed population of human HSCs and MPPs where the correlation between mRNA and protein, particularly for genes critical for stem-cell maintenance, such as quiescence and telomere maintenance, was markedly reduced compared to more- committed progenitor populations (Amon et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on human HSCs and MPPs.

claim: HSCs have reduced levels of ubiquitylated proteins and misfolded proteins, and these levels are sensitive to increased rates of translation.
source: Signer and co-workers recently reported the reduction of ubiquitylated proteins and misfolded proteins in HSCs and that these levels are sensitive to increased rates of translation (Hidalgo San Jose et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study by Signer and colleagues.

claim: Increasing levels of misfolded proteins can result in proteasomal stress and elicit the unfolded protein response in HSCs.
source: They also demonstrate that increasing levels of misfolded proteins can result in proteasomal stress and elicit the unfolded protein response.
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to the study by Signer and colleagues.

claim: Proteins associated with monoubiquitination are less abundant in HSCs.
source: Our dataset reveals that proteins associated with the monoubiquitination are less abundant in HSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene set enrichment analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Proteasomal degradation is not a major contributing factor to reduced protein levels in young adult mouse HSCs.
source: While these data indicate that proteasomal degradation is not a major contributing factor to reduced protein levels, at least in young adult mouse HSCs, they do not take into account the possibility of lysosomal degradation, which has previously been demonstrated to be important in neural stem cell maintenance and quiescence (Leeman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the data on ubiquitination and comparison to previous studies on protein degradation.

claim: Lysosomal degradation has been demonstrated to be important in neural stem cell maintenance and quiescence.
source: While these data indicate that proteasomal degradation is not a major contributing factor to reduced protein levels, at least in young adult mouse HSCs, they do not take into account the possibility of lysosomal degradation, which has previously been demonstrated to be important in neural stem cell maintenance and quiescence (Leeman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on lysosomal degradation in neural stem cells.

claim: The Mann laboratory reported the use of mass spectrometry instrumentation capable of increased sensitivity and improved proteomic coverage from no more than 200 ng (~7000 cells).
source: Recently the Mann laboratory reported the use of mass spectrometry instrumentation capable of increased sensitivity and improved proteomic coverage from no more than 200 ng (~7000 cells), dramatically improving the feasibility of performing large-scale proteomics studies on low-abundant cell types (Meier et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on mass spectrometry technology.

claim: Samples for mass spectrometry analysis were prepared with a minimum of 50,000 cells.
source: Samples for mass spectrometry analysis were prepared with a minimum of 50,000 cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental approach.

claim: For all young and old adult mouse HSCs, at least three biological cohorts of mice were utilized for each cell type, and the sample was run in technical duplicate with 200 ng (~7000 cells) of loading material per replicate.
source: For all young and old adult mouse HSCs, at least three biological cohorts of mice were utilized for each cell type, and the sample was run in technical duplicate with 200 ng (~7000 cells) of loading material per replicate.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental design.

claim: Six replicates were acquired for each of the eight young adult stem and progenitor cell types and old mouse HSCs.
source: In total, six replicates were acquired for each of the eight young adult stem and progenitor cell types and old mouse HSCs, and four replicates for each of the three old MPPs were utilized.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental design.

claim: Four replicates for each of the three old MPPs were utilized.
source: In total, six replicates were acquired for each of the eight young adult stem and progenitor cell types and old mouse HSCs, and four replicates for each of the three old MPPs were utilized.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental design.

claim: After performing mass spectrometry analysis in sextuplicate, diminishing returns on additional replicates in the context of new protein discovery were observed.
source: After performing mass spectrometry analysis in sextuplicate, we saw diminishing returns on additional replicates in the context of new protein discovery, minimizing the likelihood that differences in proteomic diversity are artifactual or a result of differential data quality (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1C on protein discovery across replicates.
